Timber Sectional Committee, CED 9 



FOREWORD 

This Indian Standard was adopted by the Bureau of Indian Standards, after the draft finalized 
by the Timber Sectional Committee had been approved by the Civil Engineering Division 
Council. 

Various Indian Standards have been formulated on different varieties on wooden furniture and 
cabinet making, namely, chairs, tables, almirahs, sofa sets etc. These specifications do not 
contain list of species to be used for the purpose, but refer to IS 399 : 1963 'Classification of 
commercial timbers and their zonal distribution { revised y for the same, which lists zonewise 
species for furniture and cabinets on the basis of general utilisation pattern in India and 
not on technical consideration for different furniture items. It also does not classify species for 
different types of furniture as the requirement of different type of furniture is different. 

Due to acute shortage of the traditionally accepted timber species and owing to the fact that 
knowledge of properties and utilization characteristics of large number of species are now 
available as a result of research carried out at Forest Research Institute, Dehra Dun, it was consi- 
dered necessary to formulate a separate comprehensive standard on classification of Indian 
timbers for furniture and cabinets as has been done for door and window shutters and frames 
( IS 12896 : 1990 ^Classification for Indian timbers for door and window shutters and frames' ). 

Requirements of timber for different types of furniture and cabinets are different. For example, 
for decorative and ornamental furniture, grain orientation, texture, colour and figure are 
important requirements. While for general utility furnitures these are not so essential. This 
classification is based on strength coeflBcient, weight, retention of shape, refractoriness to 
seasoning, ease of working, grain, colour, texture, finish, polish, general appearance etc and 
is adopted from the publication 'Classification and grading of Indian timbers for furniture and 
cabinet making' by S. S. Rajput and V. K. Gupta, Division of Forest Products, Forest Research 
Institute, Dehra Dun in the Journal of Timber Development Association ( India ), Vol 38, 
No. 1, 1992. This standard recommends 103 species in 4 groups and also lays down general 
requirement of quality of timber for furniture and cabinets. 



IS 13622 : 1993 



Indian Standard 

INDIAN TIMBERS FOR FURNITURES AND 
CABINETS — CLASSIFICATION 



1 SCOPE 

This standard covers the general classification 
of Indian Timber species suitable for furniture 
and cabinets. It also lays down the general 
requirements of quality, moisture content and 
preservative treatment for the timber. 



2 REFERENCES 

The following Indian Standards are 
adjuncts to this standard:

3 TERMINOLOGY 

3.1 For the purpose of this standard, the defini- 
tions given in IS 707 : 1976 and the following 
shall apply. 

3.2 Strength Coefficient 

The numerical value for a timber species 
evaluated by taking into consideration its 
strength as a beam, suitability as a post, reten- 
tion of shape and splitting coefficient expressed 
in terms of teak as 100. 

4 TIMBER SPECIES 

4.1 Timber for manufacture of furniture and 
cabinets shall have adequate strength, weight, 
retention of shape, ease of working, ability to 
season well, smooth finish, colour, texture, 



figure and appearance. Retention of shape 
value shall be more than 60 compared to teak 
as 100 for all timbers suitable for furniture and 
cabinets. Timber species shall be classified 
into the four groups in accordance v/ith the 
criteria given in 4.1.1 to 4.1.4, for individual 
groups. However, there are some exceptions 
for species otherwise well accepted in a 
particular group. 

4.1.1 Super Group 

The criteria for selection of species in this 
group shall be as follows: 

Strength coefficient — 75 or more 

Weight ( compared to — §5 to 110 

teak as 100 ) 

Grain, texture, finish, — Excellent 

polish and general appearance 

Species of this group are given in Annex A. 

4.1.2 Group I 

The criteria for selection of species in this 
group shall be as follows: 

Strength coefficient — 75 or more 

Weight ( compared to ~ 85 to 110 

teak as 100 ) 

Grain, texture, finish, — Very good 

polish and general appearance 

Species of this group are given in Annex B. 

4.1.3 Group II 

The criteria for selection of species in this 
group shall be as follows: 

Strength coefficient — 65 or more 

Weight ( compared to — 70 to 120 

teak as 100 ) 

Grain, texture, finish, — Good 

polish and general appearance 

Species of this group are given in Annex C. 

4.1.4 Group III 

The criteria for selection of species in this 
group shall be as follows: 



1 



IS 13622 : 1993 



Strength coefficient — 50 or more 

Weight ( compared to — 60 to 130 

teak as 100 ) 

Grain, texture, finish, — Satisfactory 

polish and general appearance 

Species of this group are given in Annex D. 

5 GENERAL REQUIREMENT 

5.1 Timber of all groups shall be free from 
decay, fungal growth, shakes, box heart, pitch 
pockets, streaks, dead and loose knots and 
insect attack. 

5.2 Following defects shall be permitted to the 
extent mentioned against each. 

5.2.1 Slope of Grain 

Slope of grain shall be permitted up to 1 in 15. 

5.2.2 Live Knots 

Live knots up to 15 mm in diameter and 2 in 
number per metre shall be permitted provided 
they are not so grouped or located as to adver- 
sely affect the strength. Live knots from 15 to 
25 mm in diameter shall be permitted to the 
extent of 1 knot per metre. The knot shall 
not be allowed near joints. 

5.2.3 Checks 

Checks up to 2 mm in depth shall be allowed. 



5.2.4 Splits 

The largest splits at both ends added together 
shall be allowed to the extent ofS percent of 
length of the piece. 

5.2.5 Bow and Spring 

These shall be allowed to the extent of 1 mm 
per metre. 

5.2.6 Cup 

Cup shall be allowed to the extent of 2 mm 
per 300 mm. 

5.2.7 Wane 

Wane shall not be more than 4 percent of the 
surface at which it appears and shall not be 
present m more than 25 percent pieces in a lot. 

6 SEASONING AND MOISTURE CONTENT 

Timber shall be seasoned to the moisture 
content conforming to 3.1 and 4.1 of 
IS 287 : 1973 by a suitable process specified in 
IS 1141:1973. Moisture content shall be 
determined either by oven drying method or 
by electrical moisture meter method as speci- 
fied in IS 11215 : 1991. 

7 PRESERVATIVE TREATMENT 

Sapwoodofall durable species and timber of 
durability class III shall be given a preservative 
treatment as specified in IS 401 : 19&2.

Standard Mark 

The use of the Standard Mark is governed by the provisions of the Bureau of Indian 
Standards Act, 1986 and the Rules and Regulations made thereunder. The Standard Mark 
on products covered by an Indian Standard conveys the assurance that they have been 
produced to comply with the requirements of that standard under a well defined system 
of inspection, testing and quality control which is devised and supervised by BIS and 
operated by the producer. Standard marked products are also continuously checked by 
BIS for conformity to that standard as a further safeguard. Details of conditions under 
which a licence for the use of the Standard Mark may be granted to manufacturers or 
producers may be obtained from the Bureau of Indian Standards. 



Bureau of Indian Standards 

BIS is a statutory institution established under the Bureau of Indian Standards Act^ 1986 to 
promote harmonious development of the activities of standardization, marking and quality 
certification of goods and attending to connected matters in the country. 

Copyright 

BIS has the copyright of all its publications. No part of these publications may be reproduced 
in any form without the prior permission in writing of BIS. This does not preclude the free use, 
in the course of implementing the standard, of necessary details, such as symbols and sizes, type 
or grade designations. E-nquiries relating to copyright be addressed to the" Director 
( Publications ), BIS. 

Revision of Indian Standards 

Amendments are issued to standards as the need arises on the basis of comments. Standards 
are also revieA^ed periodically; a standard along with amendments is reaffirmed when such review 
indicates that no changes are needed; if the review indicates that changes are needed, it is taken 
up for revision. Users of Indian Standards should ascertain that they are in possession of the 
latest amendments or edition by referring to the latest issue of 'BIS Handbook * and 'Standards 
Monthly Additions'. Comments on this Indian Standard may be sent to BIS giving the following 
reference:
